findings.text: Two helpers compute effective allowed intervals for numeric attributes from a policy entry. The unsigned form covers narrow to wide unsigned widths plus millisecond, generic unsigned, big-endian and binary-length cases; the signed form covers narrow to wide signed widths plus generic signed. Both start from width-implied extremes then apply the policy selector for fixed interval, indirect interval, lower bound only, upper bound only, or no further narrowing.

Two thin entry points expose validation-only and validation-plus-table-fill parsing of an attribute stream. Both delegate to a shared worker that walks the stream up to a maximum type, applies an optional policy table, honors validation flags, reports through an extended acknowledgement carrier, and optionally populates an indexed result table.

A small utility family supports attribute handling: linear search for first attribute of a given type; bounded copy into caller memory with zero fill for short sources; length-aware memory and string comparisons that treat trailing terminators as non-significant; duplication of payload as a terminated heap string; and safe copy into fixed caller buffers with truncation signalling.

Message construction offers reserve, put and append operations in three shapes: normal attributes with type and length header, 64-bit aligned attributes with optional pad attribute, and headerless raw payload extents. Each shape has an unchecked form that assumes space and a checked form that fails when tail room is insufficient, with distinct failure signals for pointer versus status returns.

A sizing helper estimates total wire footprint for a run of policy entries by summing aligned contributions, preferring an explicit per-entry length when present and otherwise consulting fixed-size then minimum-size tables indexed by attribute kind.

A byte search routine scans a caller-bounded memory region for the first occurrence of a given byte value, returning its address when found and a null indicator when the bound expires without a match.

Three related interfaces coordinate cross-CPU diagnostic dumps: a mask-driven trigger that handles the local CPU inline and asks other CPUs to dump via caller-supplied raise callback, a per-CPU handler that emits registers or stack and clears its pending bit, and a convenience wrapper that forwards a mask and exclusion to architecture trigger logic.

Three accessors expose aggregation object state without mutation: one resolves the effective root-owned private area even when called on a nested member, one returns the delta-owned private area only for non-root members and null for roots, and one returns a pointer to the stored key bytes.
The aggregation implementation enables tracepoint definition within its translation unit via a preprocessor marker placed before other includes.

Integer range validation branches on attribute numeric kind, sending unsigned widths, generic unsigned, milliseconds, binary length and big-endian forms to an unsigned checker and signed widths plus generic signed to a signed checker, rejecting any other kind as invalid and warning on unexpected dispatch.

The unsigned checker materializes a wide comparable value by width-appropriate decoding with network-to-host conversion for big-endian kinds and payload length for binary kind, fetches the effective interval, then fails values outside the interval with range status and distinct diagnostics for binary size versus numeric cases.

Effective unsigned intervals start from width-implied maxima with zero minimum, grouping 8-bit, 16-bit-like including binary and big-endian 16, 32-bit-like including big-endian 32, and 64-bit-like widths. Fixed-interval selectors replace both ends, indirect selector copies an externally stored interval, min-only and max-only selectors adjust one end, and other selectors leave defaults unchanged while warning on unknown widths.

Effective signed intervals start from width-implied minima and maxima for 8, 16, 32 and 64-bit-like widths, with 64-bit and generic signed sharing the widest span. Fixed, indirect, min-only and max-only selectors adjust ends analogously to the unsigned case, other selectors preserve defaults, and unknown widths warn without further update.

The signed checker decodes the payload by signed width into a wide signed comparable, fetches the effective signed interval, and fails values outside that interval with range status and a diagnostic tied to policy and attribute.

Mask validation accepts only unsigned-like and big-endian widths, decoding to a comparable with byte-order conversion where needed and rejecting other kinds. It fails when any bit outside the policy-permitted mask is set, attaching a diagnostic about reserved bits to the offending attribute.

Single-attribute validation first enforces length minima derived from explicit policy length or kind-specific minimum tables, rejecting unsupported attribute kinds when strict unknown handling is requested. It then dispatches on validation selector to no-op, integer interval checks, mask check, or caller-supplied callback, propagating the first failure and reporting policy failures with attribute-linked diagnostics.

For binary attributes under the warn-on-excessive-length selector, an over-maximum length emits a rate-limited kernel notice naming the current task and attribute kind. Strict-attribute validation still fails in that situation, while non-strict validation accepts without consulting the lower bound on the assumption that bounds are ordered.

String-oriented helpers normalize payload length by discarding at most one trailing zero byte before further work. Safe copy into caller buffers always fills the whole destination with zero padding beyond copied bytes, returns copied length on success and an oversize status when truncation was required, and rejects zero destination size or implausibly large destinations. Duplication allocates exactly normalized length plus terminator and always terminates.

Unchecked reservation advances the message tail by the aligned size, records type and length header fields, and zeroes alignment padding; headerless reservation appends a zeroed aligned extent without header. Checked reservation and put forms first compare available tail room against the required aligned size, returning null or message-size status on shortage without mutating the message. The 64-bit forms account for extra alignment padding when deciding sufficiency.

Memory comparison first orders by length difference and only compares bytes when lengths match. String comparison trims trailing zeros from the attribute payload before length ordering and likewise compares bytes only on equal trimmed length, yielding zero only for exact matches.

The injection callback resolves its container from the notifier block, scans the action list for a value match, logs when a non-zero configured error is selected, and converts the error to a notifier return code. Companion debugfs accessors clamp written wide values into the negated maximum-error to zero interval for storage and expose the stored signed value on read.

Reference counts increment and decrement by one and are returned to callers. Statistics increment and decrement both total user count and delta user count on the target, additionally adjusting the parent delta count when a parent exists. Root determination is by absence of a parent pointer, reflecting lack of nesting support.

Hint lookup yields null immediately when no hint manager exists and otherwise performs a fast hash lookup with stored parameters. Live-object lookup performs the analogous fast hash lookup in the object table.

Test aggregation policy accepts only child identifiers at or above the parent identifier and within a bounded difference. Creation enforces that check, allocates a delta record holding the identifier difference, counts the allocation in test world state, and reports invalid argument or out-of-memory failures distinctly.

Aggregation state uses two parallel designs for hints and live objects. Each manager holds operations, hash table plus parameters, ordered list, counts and identifier allocation or hint linkage. Each node or object entry embeds hash linkage, list linkage, parent pointer, root identifier, statistics and trailing flexible key bytes, with objects adding a union for delta versus root private data and a reference count covering direct and nested users.

Error-injection configuration pairs a numeric notifier value with a signed error and a human-readable action name. A container holds a notifier block followed by a flexible array of such actions that must end with an all-zero sentinel, and a helper macro fills name and value fields for a named action.

The trigger proceeds through single-flight acquisition, mask duplication with optional exclusion, inline local dump when the local CPU is targeted, announcement plus stall snapshot and remote raise when work remains, timed polling with watchdog touches until the mask drains or the timeout expires, late-responder warning plus stall check, log flush, and finally flag release and CPU release.

Parent search iterates live objects in list order, skipping non-root candidates because nesting is unsupported, and attempts aggregation into each root until one accepts. Single-parent assignment requires the candidate to be a root, asks operations to create delta state, and on success links the child, stores delta private data, optionally takes a parent reference, and emits a trace event; allocation or rejection failures leave the child unlinked.
Module initialization creates a dedicated directory for notifier error injection under the debug filesystem, while module exit recursively removes that directory and its children.

Cross-CPU trigger serialization relies on atomic test-and-set of a single global flag bit, with losers returning immediately without emitting diagnostics. Per-CPU handling serializes output against other CPUs through a print-oriented CPU synchronization section that permits nested backtrace entries from the same CPU.

Late or silent CPUs do not block indefinitely; after the bounded wait the trigger warns about the remaining mask and runs a stall check. On the handler side, an idling CPU whose registers indicate idle execution may skip register and stack emission based on a global idle-reporting flag, while still clearing its pending bit and reporting that it handled the request.
The maximum wait for remote CPUs to complete their backtrace dump is ten seconds, expressed as a compile-time constant used to size the millisecond polling loop and the late-responder warning.
